title: CHAPTER SEVEN. On Sacred Scripture's sense and interpretation
english:
CHAPTER SEVEN
On Sacred Scripture's sense and interpretation
So far concerning clarity: next comes sense. Sense is Sacred Scripture's property by which its letter agrees most exactly with the Holy Spirit's intention.

Sacred Scripture's letter is like a body, or an outward bodily sign, by which God's kingdom — which is in power or virtue (1 Cor. 4:20) — is declared to our grasp. Sense is like the vital spirit and soul by which the author's mind is set, as it were, in the open and expressed to the life by a spiritual and effectual demonstration (1 Cor. 2:4). Apart from that sense, the letter of Scripture is not God's,    but yourss — just as a king's image cast in gold is not the king's but a dog's, if that very gold is melted by fire and cast into a dog's image, as Irenaeus somewhere argues against heretical interpretations.

Here let the Enthusiast be kept far off — the one who utterly spurns Scripture, the sacred letter, and the outward word that is taught, and sets his own speculations and phantasms before it, not without an opinion of singular holiness. Blessed Luther prophesied of such in his Table Talk under the title on fanatics and sects, and the most learned Philip Marnix solidly refuted them.

title: Against a multiplex sense in one utterance; only the literal sense is the Spirit's
english: Becanus (Manual 1.1 q.3) is wont to say a double sense of Scripture is distinguished — one literal or historical, the other spiritual or mystical. Craftily put. For Protestants are not disputing here (1) whether some of the fathers acknowledged a multiplex sense of Scripture — that is nothing to the point; nor (2) whether theologians busy with interpretation may variously accommodate one and the same place — we do not deny that they may, though we do not assert that they must everywhere; nor (3) whether in diverse axioms and places one word may bear several significations — that we grant with a free hand; nor (4) whether certain things contain a mystical and typical sense — for we grant that some things are written which according to the letter report what is a type of another thing (Gal. 4:24; John 3:14; Matt. 12:40).

The question is this: whether one and the same word — not thing — in one and the same place, in one and the same part of an utterance, from the Holy Spirit's intention (not from a man's ingenious collection or arbitrary application), can have several senses besides the literal, three or four. That the papists affirm; we deny: (1) because only from the literal sense, dug out by the norms of true interpretation (which the scholion on Aph. 2 will soon teach), are true, solid, and firm arguments drawn to confirm any dogma of the faith; (2) because the literal sense alone, explained in the aforesaid way, is the Holy Spirit's sense, as the Jesuits themselves confess in Bellarmine, On the Word of God 3.3 §1.

title: II. Interpretation defined; Spirit's intent; papal breast-reliquary claim; Vincent of Lérins
english: II. Interpretation is Scripture's property by which its genuine sense — the sense most fitting to the mind and intention of the Holy Spirit as author, however that sense is uttered — is solidly and clearly shown in the earnest struggle between spirit and flesh, when the right instruments and hermeneutical rules are used.

The Holy Spirit's intention is what just interpretation seeks, and what the whole Christian world is busy digging out of the sacred letters; yet it is not obvious to all, for the reason the Apostle gives in 1 Cor. 2:14. The papists seek it in the breast-reliquary and infallibility of the Roman pontiff, to whom alone they finally defer the right of interpreting and determining Scripture's sense. Pistorius in his Guide (p. 76) concludes that no other medium of understanding Scripture is found, or is sought in vain, except in the church. Conrad Kling explains the ambiguity: as Scripture heard from a man teaches, so one must stand by the just interpretation and judgment of a man — that is, of the Church or of Peter's See. Others set other precipices of error before those who would understand Scripture. Vincent of Lérins (For the Antiquity of the Catholic Faith) notes that because of Scripture's own height not all receive it in one and the same sense, but one and another interpret its utterances differently, so that nearly as many opinions seem diggable from it as there are men.

title: Hermeneutic guides; five norms for proving spirits and true interpretation
english: Therefore, so that neither the Stoa, nor the Peripatetics, nor Plato's porch, nor even the light of sounder reason or the better dictate of conscience in adversaries can deny the true and certain sense of Scripture, that sense must be dug out by true and least-suspect means in the serious struggle of spirit with our flesh, according to the hermeneutical rules in Flacius Illyricus's Key of Sacred Scripture, Hyperius on forming sermons, Martinus on ready meditation of things, and Dannhauer's Idea of a Good Interpreter and of a Malignant Calumniator. Nor is every interpretation to be received rashly amid such variety of spirits who handle the sacred letters. Test the spirits whether they are of God, says the beloved disciple (1 John 4:1).

The tokens of proof — and so the norms of true interpretation — are five: (1) Sacred Scripture (Isa. 8:20; 34:16; Luke 16:29–31; John 5:39); (2) its unique orthodoxy and truth, Jesus Christ, God already incarnate (Heb. 13:8; John 20:31; Deut. 13:1–7; Matt. 24:23; 1 John 4:3); (3) these two not in bare words but in the power that consists in spirit and truth (1 Cor. 4:20; 2:4; 1 John 4:2); (4) from this anointing of the Spirit no lies follow, whether in Christian theory or practice, but the purest truth (1 John 2:27); (5) the event, when prophecies are to be interpreted, noted from history as fulfillments of predictions (Deut. 18:21; Jer. 28:5–9). By these, every mortal's theological interpretations, sayings, and writings about divine things are to be examined and proved — each according to his age, grace, and calling — and each is bound to try his own by them, to prove or disprove.

title: III–V. Two parts of interpretation; subject, object, medium; the fit interpreter
english: III. Interpretation has two parts: the sense and explanation of what is said, and the use and application to dogmas of faith and manners. Sense is that sentence which is immediately understood from the author through the text (Luther, Wittenberg ed., vol. 6, p. 516). Use is what is understood mediately (Rom. 15:4; 2 Tim. 3:16).
IV. In explaining the sense three things are to be observed: subject, object, and medium. If these three stand rightly, interpretation cannot fail to be just, and the truth is dug from the deep.
V. The subject is a fit interpreter, in whom two things come up for consideration: condition and instruction. The former holds the interpreter's state; the latter, his habit.

title: VI–X. Interpreter's regeneration; languages; incorrupt judgment; will free of vicious affections
english: VI. The interpreter's condition is his regeneration and illumination wrought by the Holy Spirit, whom the heavenly Father gives to those who ask (Luke 11:13; 1 Cor. 2:10–16; Jas. 1:5, 17; 2 Tim. 2:15). From this one gathers how rare good interpreters are, and how many thrust themselves into this divine office with more boldness than wisdom. Physicians promise what belongs to physicians; craftsmen handle craftsmen's tools; Scripture alone is the art everyone claims. We write poems, learned and unlearned, everywhere. A chatty old woman, a raving old man, a wordy sophist — the whole world presumes upon it, tear it, teach it before they learn it, as Jerome complains to Paulinus.

VII. Instruction is of intellect, judgment, and will. VIII. The intellect must be perfected by knowledge of the necessary languages and of the things that a discipline sets out by a sure method. Knowledge of languages is necessary for the interpreter (1 Cor. 14:13–14), because each has its properties that must be carefully noted in translating. Hence the Egyptians are praised for learning the Canaanites' tongue (Isa. 19:18). It is absurd for the Holy Spirit's language to be to the interpreter like a flute that makes a sound but without mind — and for the prophet to be to a German like a Turk or an Indian, to each of whom the other is a barbarian. Jerome and Augustine knew this of old; among later writers Luther, and Bellarmine himself, affirms that Augustine was deceived by mere ignorance of Hebrew. An encyclopedia of things supplies the needed knowledge and the way of knowing and teaching (Titus 1:9; Col. 2:4).

IX. A good interpreter's judgment should be uncorrupted, aiming straight at the truth (1 Tim. 5:21; Gal. 2:14). Monkish theology, by contrast, sees nothing in the Scriptures but cowls and wooden shoes, as Luther testifies. X. The sacred interpreter's will should be free from vicious affections, lest against the intellect's dictate he calumniate the truth.

title: XI. Object is the coherent biblical text; Hebrew and Greek authentic norms
english: XI. The object is the biblical text cohering with itself in its whole series. Clement of Alexandria (Stromata 7) calls the text the body and fabric of God's prophecy, in which, as subject-matter, words are considered, and in the words a proper or tropical signification, from which the sense is so drawn that the interpreter permits neither himself to be severed from the text, nor words from the text, nor sense from the words. Sense is one thing, signification another. The former belongs to whole utterances; the latter to single words. Sense is drawn from the nature and order of the words as they regard one another in Scripture's sayings, and is perfected by the Holy Spirit alone — whose alone is true interpretation, just as in civil law the interpretation of statutes belongs to him who constituted them.

Further: the Hebrew text of the Old Testament, furnished and corrected with Masoretic notes as preserved by us Christians in approved copies (even Jewish ones), is so free from all corruption — whether of diction and sentences or of letters and points — that it is the divine NORM, canon, and rule by which all versions in other tongues, and especially the Latin Vulgate, ought to be examined and emended. The Greek text of the New Testament, preserved in approved codices, is likewise so free from corruptions that it is the most exact norm by which all versions and interpretations ought to be examined and corrected. Glassius demonstrates this at length in Sacred Philology, Book 1, tracts 1 and 2.

title: Versions useful but not ultimate; against Targum prophecy and Trent's Vulgate authenticity
english: Versions may indeed be used in settling theological controversies, but not ultimately. Theodoret notes that the Scriptures have been turned not only into Greek but into Roman, Egyptian, Persian, Indian, Armenian, Scythian, and even Sarmatian — once for all, as I may say, into all the tongues the nations have used — and that for our teaching, as Paul teaches (Rom. 15:4). Yet if a laborious and more solid investigation of the truth is to be undertaken, and appeal is made by due process from versions to the original text, then one must flee to no version, but to the Hebrew and Greek truth alone, as to a citadel and stronghold, with Jerome in his letter to Vitalis. For a prophet is one thing, an interpreter another, as Jerome says in the preface to the Pentateuch, calling authentic Scripture itself the truth.

Therefore (1) the Jews err who ascribe prophetic authority to the Chaldean paraphrast; (2) the papists err who make the Latin Vulgate authentic — Trent, session 4, decreeing that the old Vulgate edition be held authentic in public readings, disputations, preachings, and expositions. Yet Arias Montanus, one of the Tridentine fathers, thinks otherwise in his preface to the Biblical work. To him for instruction we commend Martin Becanus, who too awkwardly praises his party's happiness in following one certain, constant, and uniform edition.

title: XII–XVIII. Threefold medium: before the thing, in the thing, after the thing
english: XII. The medium of interpretation is threefold: one before the thing, another in the thing, a third after the thing. XIII. Before the thing, first to be regarded in the text under interpretation — and in all Sacred Scripture — is the harmony of the text and the analogy of faith; then the leading of pious and learned interpreters who explained the text before us is not wholly to be despised. Polanus: the analogy of faith is nothing other than Scripture's constant and perpetual sentence in open and least obscure places — such as the articles of faith in the Apostles' Creed, collected from Scripture in so many words; such as are contained in the Decalogue, the Lord's Prayer, and other plain texts. Interpretation ought to be made according to this (Rom. 12:6; 2 Tim. 1:13). Nor is the leading of orthodox interpreters wholly to be scorned, as Augustine testifies On the Usefulness of Believing.

XIV. In the thing is the medium that actually enters the explanation of the text and draws its sense from itself. XV. It is either notional or real. XVI. Notional is what turns on the words, phrases, and idioms of the language — here belong criticism, the author's style, and elucidation by metaphrase and paraphrase. XVII. Real is what turns on the thing and its circumstances, on the context and aim, and the rest. For as a building is weak without a foundation, so unless the aim is found Scripture is useless, as Chrysostom testifies. XVIII. After the thing is the comparison of parallel places. From this no small part of hermeneutical harmony emerges. Whoever wants more may see, among other works, Dannhauer's Idea of a Good Interpreter.

title: XIX–XXIII. Use and application; didactic vs critical interpretation; ordinary didactic
english: XIX. The use and application of things is that by which they are related to the sense and norm of sound words expressed by fallible signs from the Spirit's purpose and will, are set forth; catholic dogmas are properly explained and confirmed; heterodox and false things are solidly and vigorously confuted; corrupt manners are amended; good things are commanded; the sorrowful and faint-hearted are raised up; the secure and bold are terrorstruck — so that the man of God may be made perfect and furnished for every good work. The foundation of this interpretation stands in 2 Tim. 3:16; Rom. 15:4; Jude 20–23.

XX. Next, interpretation is either didactic or critical (judicial). Bellarmine admits this distinction (On the Word of God 3.10, reply to argument 16). XXI. Didactic interpretation is what is done as by a teacher, with fit reasons skillfully applied, according to the catholic and manifest laws of interpreting. XXII. It is either ordinary or extraordinary. XXIII. Ordinary is what rests on equivalence or consequence that has no controversy, or that at least has agreeing and notorious testimony from the primitive Church.

title: Consequences of Scripture; extraordinary prophetic interpretation
english: Some papists little favor this. Forerus calls consequences futile glosses; Veronius says consequences are not the pure Word of God but something drawn by the intellect's discourse from the Word of God. But these men, as they are absurd, so they also contradict Bellarmine, who notes that when the Nicene council defined Christ to be homoousios with the Father, it was for no other reason than that Scripture says the Son is God — from which it NECESSARILY FOLLOWS that Father and Son are of the same substance and deity. Likewise, as in law what is truly and duly deduced from statutes by good consequence is received by jurists no less than what lies there in formal words, so what is truly and duly deduced from Scripture by good consequence is assumed by theologians as itself intended by the Holy Spirit.

We are secure that the Word of God and consequences differ. Consequences can be considered in two ways: (1) in themselves, abstractly and formally — and so they are human and are judged by Aristotle; (2) in and with the matter to which they are applied, so that they coalesce, as it were, with a sacred and infallibly true thing — and so they are not human. The firm rule is: from two premises, one natural and one revealed, there follows a conclusion that cannot be known naturally. XXIV. Extraordinary interpretation is what rests on some authentic and undoubted knowledge and truth of the interpreter, even of one alone. This is wholly infallible — as when God himself by later words teaches what he meant by earlier ones, and when the Apostles with extraordinary and prophetic certainty explain what the sense of the old prophets is.

title: XXV–XXVIII. Critical/judicial interpretation; its didactic core; assessor's help
english: XXV. Critical or judicial interpretation is that by which, as by a judge's sentence, law is fitted with authority to a fact, a rule to an example, a universal precept to singular cases. Examples: 2 Sam. 12:5, when David is pronounced guilty of death because every murderer is guilty of death; 1 Tim. 1:20, when Hymenaeus is pronounced a son of Satan because every heretic is a son of Satan. Such interpretation cannot be done by the law, which is not laid down about singulars, but is left to the judge as judge, who pronounces about singulars according to the law.

XXVI. Judicial interpretation is commonly joined with didactic. So when it is asked whether Hymenaeus is a heretic, he is condemned of heresy because he denies the future resurrection. But the Scripture places that speak of the resurrection of the flesh were to be understood not of a spiritual rising from sins only, as Hymenaeus seems to have taken them, but of the resurrection from the dead properly so called. That interpretation was so clear and certain, handed down by the Apostles themselves, that it could not be denied without open malice and obstinacy (2 Tim. 2:17–18).

XXVII. This interpretation that unfolds the sense of the text or rule is indeed required for the judge's sentence and concurs with it, and so by a certain metonymy of the adjunct can be called judicial; yet properly and formally it is not judicial but didactic — which the judge offers not as a judge having power to fit law to fact, but as a teacher understanding the law's sense by equivalence or consequence or some authentic knowledge. XXVIII. But if the judge lacks knowledge and doctrine, this didactic interpretation can and ought to be supplied by another more skilled — namely, the judge's assessor and counselor.

title: XXIX. Papal claims on councils and Pope; three remaining questions
english: XXIX. Further, judicial interpretation in the Papacy is ascribed partly to a council, partly to the Roman Pontiff, partly to both together. For only the greater prelates — that is, bishops — ordinarily have decisive suffrage in councils; by privilege and custom also cardinals and general abbots of orders, even if not bishops; to laity and to uncalled priests, none; to those and to lesser clerics helping in debate they grant only consultative suffrage, as Bellarmine teaches. On which councils and how far they can err in interpretation, the papists disagree among themselves.

Three questions remain: (1) Can a council err without the Pontiff or before his confirmation? (2) Can the Pontiff err? (3) Is the Pope above a council? Bellarmine (On Councils 2.17) holds that the Pontiff is simply and absolutely above the universal Church and above a general council. But this is a claimed right — indeed pure ambition — the Hildebrandine claim thrust into the church some years ago. From which we gather: about judicial interpretation properly so called (fitting law to fact) there is no controversy, because both sides confess that councils and the Pontiff can err in a question of fact; the controversy that remains is about didactic interpretation.

title: Infallible didactic interpretation only when Scripture-bound; no new revelations
english: For the papists want interpretation to be infallible and binding on all Christians whenever the Pontiff either decides something with a general council or, without one, teaches from the chair — that is, whenever as Pontiff he defines what is to be believed by all, whether a reason from the Scriptures appears or not. We grant that interpretation is infallible and binding whenever a council, or even any single bishop and doctor of the Church, offers an interpretation that rests on evident equivalence, or on catholic and among Christians undoubted consequence, or on extraordinary or prophetic authority sufficiently demonstrated — as we taught in Aphorisms 23 and 24.

But since extraordinary interpretation is not given in the Church today — for she is not ruled by new revelations but remains in what was once delivered, as Bellarmine himself confesses — therefore one must look to the first two, and because this interpretation is properly didactic, in the ordinary way it is to be followed only so far as reason persuades. So if an interpretation of Scripture is brought without catholic consent, or the Church's consent without the Scriptures, that opinion may indeed be probable; yet not such as ought to be proposed to the church and pressed as catholic and necessarily to be believed.

title: Reasons against papal sole interpreter; circular argument; triune interpretive principle
english: The reasons for our judgment are these. (1) We must continually fear what is said in Prov. 30:5–6: Every word of God is purified: it is a shield to those who take refuge in him. Do not add to his words, lest he rebuke you and you be found a liar. Therefore no one ought in interpreting to put forward anything there is danger of addition, nor propose as God's infallible word what he is not again and again sure carries no charge of falsehood from himself. (2) Eccl. 5:2–3: do not speak rashly, and let not your heart be swift to utter a word before God; God is in heaven, you on earth; therefore let your words be few. (3) Above all the anathema spoken by Paul against those who evangelize anything beyond what he had evangelized must be dreaded (Gal. 1:8–9).

Against the Jesuits who say only the Pontiff holds infallible authority to interpret the Scriptures, one must proceed thus: their argument in form commits a circle and begs the principle. Let the rule be noted: whatever the Holy Spirit teaches through canonical Scripture in the serious struggle is of infallible and most certain truth, in which the conscience can safely rest as on a rock (Matt. 7:24–25). This is the triune principle of all theological interpretation. Scripture indeed contains the truth by itself, but without the Spirit it is not rightly understood, and without the Spirit's power (1 Cor. 2:4) it is discerned only in the struggle against flesh and Satan (Gal. 5:17; Eph. 6:12), according to each person's age and capacity (1 Cor. 3:2).

title: XXX. Six illegitimate measures of sense (Vulgate, old Adam, fathers, traditions, pope, no age-care)
english: XXX. From what we have taught so far we rightly infer that an interpretation is weak and not solid enough or legitimate which is made (1) according to the sense as canonized in the Vulgate version — because it strikes against the object of legitimate interpretation: that version is not authentic, nor even the text the interpreter ought first to interpret; (2) according to the sense as it depends on old Adam's reason — because Sacred Scripture's sense stands above that reason and is measured by God's Spirit and the will of its writer; (3) according to the sense as measured by the fathers' sense — because then the text that bears sense from itself would be neglected; because either all the fathers' sense or only some would be the rule — neither works; because it conflicts with hermeneutical laws that acknowledge the fathers as guides, not as infallible; because they often missed the genuine sense; because they not rarely followed erroneous senses; (4) according to the sense as completed by unwritten traditions; (5) according to the sense as determined by the Church or by the Pope, for the same reasons we gave at Aph. 26; (6) without distinguishing childish and mature age, milk and solid food, which the Apostle wisely observes in teaching (1 Cor. 3:1–2; Heb. 5:12–14).

title: Solid food of Scripture; XXXI–XXXII public and private interpretive power; Cap. 7 close
english: Solid food is contained chiefly in these four: (1) the true and certain accommodation of the prophets to their defined times, places, things, and persons; (2) the exact and full reduction of Levitical shadows to their body and truth exhibited in the New Testament; (3) the fitting application of the divine governance typified through all Scripture to its truth; (4) the neat and undoubted explanation of the whole created universe — which is its Creator's image, and in which the letter, parables, and phrases of all Sacred Scripture lie ready — to its truth described in the same place.

XXXI. The power of interpreting and judging is twofold: public or private. Both rest on vocation and a singular gift. XXXII. The power of privately judging Sacred Scripture's sense in things necessary to salvation belongs to all the faithful, for confirming their own faith and edifying others, according to the law of charity, the measure of the gift received, and the diverse reason of calling. The Leiden theologians rightly draw this from the Synopsis of Purer Theology (disp. 5, th. 29) out of John 10:3; Matt. 7:15; 1 Cor. 10:15; 1 John 4:1. This kind of judging rests on the gift of discernment (1 Cor. 2:15; Heb. 5:14; Phil. 1:10).

The power of publicly judging the truth of interpretation belongs only to those who by peculiar vocation and gift of interpreting are furnished for it. The grades of this vocation are listed in Eph. 4:11; the gift is indicated in Rom. 12:6; 1 Cor. 14:3, 29. And although in every age there have also been other Christians who by prayers and assiduous reading and meditation of Sacred Scripture received the gift of interpreting the sacred letters for public uses and of proving spirits in fuller measure than some pastors; yet that gift is chiefly to be sought among those whom God has peculiarly called to teach his Church publicly (Mal. 2:6–7).
